edges.effect_quant: Prospective meta-analyses often show a small positive association between heavier coffee intake and lung-cancer incidence, but that signal weakens sharply in never-smokers and BMI-adjusted analyses.
edges.mechanism: Coffee does not have a strong, clean lung-carcinogenesis mechanism comparable to tobacco smoke, which is why confounding matters so much here. Roast-related compounds and correlated smoking behavior have both been proposed, but the persistent attenuation in better-adjusted subsets makes a direct causal interpretation doubtful.
edges.summary: At first glance the pooled literature looks harmful, with recent prospective meta-analyses reporting higher lung-cancer risk in heavier coffee drinkers. The problem is that the association shrinks toward null in never-smokers and in studies with stronger adjustment, so the safest label is contested rather than harmful per se.
edges.caveats: Coffee and smoking are tightly linked in many cohorts, making residual confounding very hard to eliminate completely. This edge should be interpreted as an epidemiologic warning about confounding more than as evidence that coffee itself drives lung cancer.
